MR. WOOLLIAMS    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege concerning a matter that is found on page 2234 of Hansard. My question of privilege, stated briefly, is that I suggest with the greatest respect that the Secretary of State misinformed the house yesterday, and did it deliberately, in respect of a question that I put to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration.
I should like to review the facts relating to this question of privilege. My question was this:
Is it not a fact that Banks was admitted to Canada by a special order in council of the previous government?
Then the Secretary of State said:
That is not a fact.
I did not have the facts with me at the time because the report of Mr. Justice Norris had just come out. I did just mention that at the time. I shall read the question of privilege I raised then:
On a question of privilege, the Secretary of State denied an assertion which I made a few minutes ago, but I have now found the reference in support of what I had to say. I wish to read from page 312 of the report of the industrial inquiry commission on the disruption of shipping:
"The order in council of July 6, 1954, which authorizes Banks' admission to Canada, was based on the fact that there was satisfactory evidence of his rehabilitation. He was granted status as a landed immigrant."
Then the Secretary of State compounded and made much graver an already grave situation because as the minister of citizenship and immigration of the former Liberal government he should have known the facts. This is what he said:
It is correct that after Mr. Banks came to live in Canada he was given the status of a landed immigrant, but he was first admitted to Canada, it seems to me, immediately after the war and not at that time.
My question of privilege is this. This is a misstatement of fact. As the former minister of citizenship and immigration in the Liberal administration, the minister knew that a person is legally admitted to Canada
when he is granted landed status. I am sure the minister was aware of that. I should like to refer to section 5 of the Immigration Act, chapter 325 of the revised statutes of Canada, which reads as follows:
No person, other than a person referred to in subsection (2) of section 7, shall be admitted to Canada if he is a member of any of the following classes of persons:
Then paragraph (d) definitely affected Banks' admission to Canada, and it reads as follows:
Persons who have been convicted of or admit having committed any crime involving moral turpitude, except persons whose admission to Canada is authorized by the governor in council upon evidence satisfactory to him...
At that time the Liberal government-that was in July, 1954-passed a special order in council admitting Banks to Canada. I suggest in this question of privilege that if that order in council were now rescinded Banks would go back from whence he came. I say the minister committed a grave misrepresentation when he misrepresented the fact that it was his government which brought Banks into Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think what the hon. gentleman has said is perhaps good evidence of the desirability of certain hon. members of the house-and I am not referring to the hon. gentleman but to myself-keeping their mouths shut. What I said was literally quite correct, that Mr. Banks was in Canada and had been in Canada for quite some time, at the time that order in council was passed. Therefore in the normal sense of the word he was not admitted, because he was here. He had been admitted as a visitor a number of years before, and had been living in Canada for several years before this question that he should be given the status of a landed immigrant came up.
I do think that when the hon. gentleman brought the matter up on a question of privilege yesterday, I explained quite accurately what the situation was. I had no intention whatsoever of misleading the house, and if in any way I did in fact mislead any hon. member of the house, or any other person in Canada, I apologize; and I accept my full share of responsibility for the order in council that was passed in 1954.

subtopic: CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES RESPECTING NATIONAL POLICY

speakeroldname: Hon. J. P. Deschatelets (Minister of Public Works):
subtopic: CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES RESPECTING NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on July 15 the Prime Minister indicated that I would make a statement as the result of a meeting which he and I had with a delegation from the Yel-lowhead route association. On July 12 the Prime Minister and I received a brief from the Yellowhead association which was presented in person by Mr. William Hawrelak as president of that association.
National Highway Policy
The brief made two main points; one, to request the federal government to establish a policy on federal aid to the provinces for the construction of main highways; and second, to recommend that in any such federal aid provision be made for the construction of the Yellowhead route as early as possible. In the past few weeks the government has received other delegations and briefs requesting that we take some action on the formulation of a national highway policy.
In reply to questions from hon. members I recently reported in this house that I had been in touch with the ministers of highways of all provinces to make arrangements for meetings between the provincial officials and officials of my department. I should like to advise the house that the purpose of these meetings with the provincial officials is to collect information, construction schedules and possible problems on the present federal-provincial highway projects as well as to receive suggestions from the provinces on what they felt would be the role of the federal government in the highway field. Over the years the federal government has received a variety of proposals for extending the federal-provincial highway arrangements, and as might be expected the desires of all areas were not always the same. The present review is to gain a picture of the provincial thinking at this stage.
I am in a position to report that discussions have taken place with the provinces of New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Ontario and in Quebec, where at this stage time has permitted dealings with only the trans-Canada highway. Discussions are at this date taking place in St. John's, Newfoundland and on the 19th in Halifax, Nova Scotia. Discussions with the western provinces are planned to start July 25.
It is our intention, once information has been collected and reviewed by the government, that I will have discussions with the ministers of highways, when we could discuss policies, but with the information obtained, based on a factual background of programs and possible expenditures. Once this has been done it is our intention to have a federal-provincial conference which would give consideration to a relationship between the federal and provincial governments in the highway field. It is hoped, subject to the reaction of the provinces, that this conference could take place this fall.
With reference to the question of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) in connection with the request for a second trans-Canada highway, I wish to say that this can be dealt with only after consultation with the provinces.

National Highway Policy

subtopic: CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES RESPECTING NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
We are pleased to have this report from the minister, and we are looking forward to the results of the proposed meeting with the various provincial governments in connection with this important matter. For a number of years we have been advocating a national highway system for Canada, and I would hope that in consequence of the broad policy which may come out of these meetings such a system of highways would be forthcoming. The participation of the national government must, I think, reflect the arrangements made with the provinces on fiscal matters. If the government of Canada is taking the lion's share of taxes it must naturally take on additional responsibilities.
Regarding the Yellowhead route, we are aware there is some confusion as to where the second trans-Canada highway may go after it passes Jasper. It has been proposed that it should turn south to Kamloops and on to Vancouver, but I should like to point out that its location should be what is known as highway 16 through to Prince Rupert down the highway which will be built simultaneously, as the province of British Columbia has stated on more than one occasion, with the highway through Tete Jaune Cache down through Blue River.
We are very interested in this project and are hoping for some real progress in connection with a highway system in Canada.

subtopic: CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES RESPECTING NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
The Minister of Public Works is to be commended for taking the preliminary step of calling together the ministers of highways of the various provinces of Canada to discuss the matter of a second trans-Canada highway. Several of the provinces have completed their portions of the first trans-Canada highway. In some cases the work was completed several years ago. They are now anxious to proceed with a second highway, and if one takes account of the increasing motor traffic in Canada one can realize how urgently it is required.
I hope two other matters will be discussed at this conference. The first is the possibility of north-south traffic of an international character. If the tourist trade is to be encouraged there should be a tremendous improvement in the highways which bring in tourist traffic. This is too large a burden for the provinces themselves to assume and it might well become a joint project. The other matter concerns the maintenance of these highways. At the present time the entire cost of maintenance falls on the provincial governments. When there was only one trans-Canada highway they could meet it, but if there is to be an enlarged area of federal participation in highway construction it seems to me some plan should be worked out for joint participation in responsibility for maintaining these roads.

1.	Is the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys carrying on any tests to determine the effect of uranium as an alloy in uranium steel alloy drills and with uro-steel pipe, cord and cable?
2.	Is the department studying possible uses for uranium in alloys with both ferrous and nonferrous metals and, if so, what have been the results of such tests and studies?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext:
Mines branch staff in co-operation with industry are pursuing a
broad program of research and development on the use of uranium as an addition agent to metals and alloys. Although very comprehensive work on the utilization of uranium in steel has been accomplished with favourable results, particularly in the refining of steel and the production of drill rod material and steel alloys for pipes, it cannot be said at this stage that a major breakthrough resulting in commercial acceptance has been achieved.

Questions
The addition of uranium to non-ferrous metals provides a refining action resulting in properties such as the improved hot workability of copper, nickel, and their respective alloys.
Briefly, it can be said that although it is too early to fully evaluate the results of studies carried but in the mines branch laboratories, there are hopeful indications that uranium is moving toward a significant nonnuclear role in industry.

1.	Has the Department of Transport licensed a wired television system in Geraldton, Ontario, and, if so, when, and to what organization (address, officers, etc.)?
2.	Has the D.O.T. checked this cable system at any time to discover if radiation from it may be affecting T.V. signals coming to residents using aerials, and, if so, when, with what results, and interpretations?

1. Two community antenna television systems have been licensed in Geraldton, Ontario:
(i)	Mr. Harry Assad-P.O. Box 1, Geraldton, Ontario, first licence issued April 29, 1960.
(ii)	Marino Hardware and Electric Co. Ltd., Box 14, Geraldton, Ontario, first licence issued April 9, 1962.
2. Yes, however, any difficulty in the reception of programs at Geraldton seems to be one of distance to the nearest television broadcasting station rather than one of interference. Geraldton is approximately 140 miles from Port Arthur and 215 miles from Marquette and accordingly it is outside the normal service area of stations WLUC-TV Marquette, Michigan and CFPA-TV Port Arthur, Ontario.
Normally the coverage for a fullpower television broadcasting station with a 500 foot antenna is considered to be out to a 57 mile radius for the low VHF band, channels 2 to 6. Satisfactory reception may be expected within this coverage area with a good outdoor antenna. Beyond this area it may be possible to locate sites, usually on relatively high ground, where television signals may be received with sufficient strength for satisfactory reception, provided a more elaborate receiving antenna and a properly aligned receiving set is used.
In some locations reception may be satisfactory on a long term basis, while at others it may be satisfactory for a while and then disappear completely for varying periods of time. These variations in reception are caused by the normal propagation characteristics of the frequencies used for television broadcasting and reception becomes more sporadic as the distance between the receiving antenna and the transmitting antenna is increased.

Mr. Harry Assad's system was inspected, following complaints, on March 28 and 29, 1962. There was some radiation at that time which was caused by the cable being repeatedly broken, by large trucks, during the winter and proper repairs could not be made due to the wintertime weather conditions. Mr. Assad was informed about appropriate corrective action to be taken. Departmental records indicate no complaints have been received since March 1962.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 23 and again on June 14 the hon. member for Brandon-Souris inquired about the appointment of the secretary general of the resources minister's council. On those occasions the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources indicated that he would inform the house at the time the appointment was made.
In my minister's absence today I can tell the hon. member, and other hon. members of the house, that the executive committee of the council has unanimously agreed to the appointment of Mr. Daniel Wermenlinger. The chairman of the Canadian resources minister's council, Hon. Rene Levesque, will be releasing a communique today concerning this appointment.
Mr. Wermenlinger was chosen from a group of 60 applicants from all parts of Canada following public advertisement. For his duties as secretary general to the Canadian resources minister's council Mr. Wermenlinger brings an excellent background as a consulting engineer and teacher. He is age 38 and is a McGill University graduate in engineering. He has had employment in the electric power industry in Quebec, and has been professor of the development of electric power at Laval University. He actively participated in the resources for tomorrow conference of 1961 and was a delegate in May, 1962 at the "conference internationale des grands reseaux electriques" in Paris.
The new secretary general will take up his duties commencing August 15, and the office of the permanent secretariat will be located in Montreal. The house resumed from Monday, July 15, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lamontagne for the second reading of Bill No. C-72, to provide for the establishment of an economic council of Canada.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND DEFINITION OF DUTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I now take up my interrupted speech of last Monday, if you can call five minutes fill-in the beginning of a speech. Since that time I have been able to read with greater care the interesting discourse of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Lamontagne) when he introduced this measure into the house. I am now more astonished than I was before I made that careful examination that the minister is prepared to stand in his place in this house and describe this strange, anaemic piece of legislation as the government's program for establishing planning in this country. Moreover, I am astonished that a gentleman of his reputed economic knowledge is prepared to stand in the chamber and tell us that this bill is going to be the basis of what is known as indicative planning. I do not for one moment imagine that the minister is not well aware of most of the circumstances surrounding the particular national planning to which the term indicative planning was first applied. I refer to the economy of France. I assume he must know what went on there; he must know what the basis of French planning is, and I am 28902-5-147
Economic Council of Canada astonished that he would tell us that his government's program is designed to introduce indicative planning into Canada.
Just in case he has not looked recently at the facts regarding the French commissariat du plan, I would like to put on the record some of the circumstances under which French planning was instituted. In the first place, it was instituted on a very widespread foundation of nationalization; all the coal mining industry, all gas and electricity, all insurance companies, all savings banks and similar savings institutions were nationalized. Specific industries, such as the Gnome-Rhone, Lorraine and Renault aviation engine factories, the Renault automobile factory and, of course, the railways have been nationalized for many years in France. In addition to that there are credit controls in operation in France, controls which I am sure this government has not in mind at all. Medium term loans must be rediscounted at the bank of France, which must consult the commissariat du plan for loans over one million francs. The Credit National, which is the main source of long-term investment funds, must consult the commissariat on all loans over two and a half million francs. In addition to that there are in effect in France quite a wide range of price controls over steel, aluminum, fuel and power, chemicals and motor cars. On top of that Mr. Speaker, there has been a wide measure of public investment in private industry, a sample of which is, of course, the steel industry, 30 per cent of the internal debt of which is held by the public authority. So we see, Mr. Speaker, that in the only instance of general indicative planning, the planning under which the term was first applied, the indicative finger is involved directly in a great many economic pies. As Mr. Pierre Masse, the commissaire general du plan, had to say at a meeting in London:
Directly or indirectly the state controls or is always the main driving influence behind one half of total investment in France.
I mention this, Mr. Speaker, to point out that the use of the term "indicative planning" for the incoherent measures proposed by this government is really grossly misleading.
I would then turn to the make-up of the commissariat du plan in France, and I am sure that if Mr. Pierre Masse, the commissaire general, were to be presented with this bill which is before the house as a sample of indicative planning, Mr. Masse would probably go into hysterics. The commission in France is composed of approximately 50 experts of various sorts. Not merely economists, agronomists and sociologists, but university people and all manner

Economic Council of Canada of people are employed on a full time basis. Even more important than that, as one of the key methods by which French indicative planning is made successful there are established under the plan a large number of commissions made up of those who are actually in control of or responsible for the operation of various sectors of the French economy. Mr. Masse says that if the real forces of the country have been associated with making the plan, they are more likely to stand together in action.
I have no knowledge, of course, of who the 25 ordinary members of this economic council are to be, but I am sure of this, that they are not going to be people such as those who are called in in France to help in the construction of a plan, the people who are actively engaged in the operation of the French economy. We shall have, I presume, someone who purports to represent organized labour, someone who purports to represent the consumers, someone who purports to represent the employers and manufacturers associations. But it will not be the people who are engaged in the actual operation of the economy. Because if it were, Mr. Speaker, you would require many more than 25. You would require a similar set-up to that which they have in France, where you have up to 30 or 40 separate commissions, which are, in effect, working parties composed of government officials, industrialists, financiers, manufacturers, people who are engaged in the operations of the economy.
Therefore I suggest that this bill, when it is presented to us as the means by which planning is to be established in Canada in the first place, is nothing but a hoax; and in particular, when it is suggested to us that on the basis of this bill we can have something which could rightly be termed indicative planning then to my mind this is grossly misleading. Nowhere at all in the bill and nowhere at all in the speech of the President of the Privy Council is there any suggestion whatever of actually setting up a planning agency. The French indicative planning is dependant upon an actual planning agency, a planning agency which, as I say, draws into its ambit various other sections of the community in active working parties to draft the plan, and the plan itself is, of course, written under the auspices of the minister of finance.
Admittedly, in Canada we have two problems facing us which do not face France, or indeed any other nation in the world where planning has taken place. One of these is the very large measure of foreign ownership of our resources and our industries. The other is the federal structure of our country. These two problems are to my mind closely linked;

in fact, one can hardly be dealt with without the other. Not too long ago the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) attempted in a most praiseworthy manner to deal with the first of these problems by bringing in an ill-starred takeover tax-not a very practical way of approaching this problem, but we can at least give him credit for making the attempt. But even if he had been successful this would not have coped with the continuing situation in Canada; it would merely have applied a brake to any further developments along this line. If the problem is to be coped with-and many seem to think it does not have to be coped with-it can only be done by replacing foreign owners by Canadian owners. However, here we run into two other problems. One is the unwillingness of the present owners to sell, and the other is the fact that if they were willing and the purchasers were private Canadian citizens, there would be no guarantee that the Canadian purchasers would not at a later date dispose of their property to foreign purchasers.
The only other manner of replacing foreign ownership by Canadian ownership is by replacing foreign owners by a public authority in Canada. Here we run into the problem of our constitution in Canada, with the provincial legislatures having control over property and civil rights. However, I think this problem is perhaps not insoluble if we had a government really prepared to do something about indicative planning and really prepared to cope with this problem of foreign ownership. But first of all we have to make up our minds about the answer to this question, which is: Do we really consider foreign ownership to be a detriment to the Canadian nation? I ask this question, Mr. Speaker, because I have found to my dismay that there are many people, some even in this chamber, who seem to regard the foreign ownership of our resources and our industry, with its inevitable result of absorption into the neighbouring republic, with a certain amount of equanimity. In this party we are convinced that foreign ownership is detrimental to our country, specifically in the context of the bill now before us.
This bill purports to be the foundation stone for indicative planning. It is impossible to carry out anything in the nature of indicative planning in the real sense of the word while this condition of extensive foreign ownership remains. Mr. Masse's comment on the necessity of drawing into the building of the plan all the real forces within the country indicates what our problem is here. What are the real forces of this country-the forces of economic power? They are not, in the main, Canadian forces. When we have to deal with these forces we have to

deal with people or institutions whose concern is not the Canadian nation or the Canadian economy, except in so far as these are the source of immediate profit or addenda to a foreign economy. So I suggest that if the government is serious about embarking on a program of indicative planning it will have to deal with this question of foreign ownership and, in doing so, deal with the situation created by the Canadian constitution.
There have been references in the press and elsewhere to the difficulties the government is encountering in connection with the Canadian constitution at the present time as well as the pressures which are being applied by the provincial governments, in particular with regard to certain economic matters, all of which have to be considered in relation to anything we could call economic planning. We hear, for instance, that the premier of Quebec is much opposed to the government's plan for a portable pension. In fact, there have been reports in the press to this effect. Of course, the premier's fundamental economic reason for opposing it-and it is a most respectable reason-is that he sees in the pension plan a means of accumulating a volume of investment capital which could be used to expand the economy of his province. I suspect Mr. Lesage has discovered something which I think I have discovered. We will have to wait until tomorrow, I suppose, when the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) makes a statement in this house before we can confirm this; but I have a suspicion that I have discovered the truth, namely, that the portable pension plan is not going to result in any pooling of the savings of the Canadian public, but that instead it is likely to provide a happy hunting ground for the insurance companies and a continuation of the means by which corporations who arrange their own pension plans avoid a large measure of corporation taxes.
I hope I am wrong. If I am, there may still be some way of instituting indicative planning in Canada within the confines of confederation. It may be we shall find we are experiencing much the same results as Sweden, a country which has some interesting lessons to offer us if we were not too timid to accept them. In the London Economist of March 20, there was an article by a Swedish financial correspondent entitled "Enter the New Leviathan". This article describes an almost revolutionary transformation which has taken place in the monetary and credit field in Sweden over the last 12 months because of the operation of the Swedish social insurance plan and the coming into 28902-5-1471
Economic Council of Canada effect of the national supplementary pension fund. This has had far reaching consequences for the capital market, and I should like to quote briefly from this article:
Although the fund did not start its operations until 1960 and will go on growing for many years to come, it has already become the prime source of long-term finance. Last year the increase in its investments amounted to 1,300 million kronor, and this year it will fall not far short of 2,000 million.
It is estimated, on fairly conservative assumptions, that the fund will have increased its resources to 25,000 million kronor by the end of this decade. This would correspond to about a quarter of all institutional credits; and its share of the market would then be the same as that of the commercial banks is today. Its annual investments would in 1970 be between 5,000 and 6,000 million kronor, equal to the total net amount of borrowings from all institutions in 1962.
I suggest that here lies a clue to dealing with two problems which in my opinion stand as an immovable barrier to any effective indicative planning in Canada, namely the existence of such an enormous degree of foreign ownership and, secondly, the difficulty of bringing the provincial authorities into any concerted national plan. I would suggest the experience in Sweden indicates the way in which the government, if it really wishes to embark on a program of planning, should be moving at this time. It should be prepared to use this portable pension plan as a means of building up a vast pool of the savings of the Canadian people and it should be prepared to make arrangements with the provincial governments so as to make available the capital they require for their own investment programs. I suggest that had this government possessed the courage and the honesty to make known a real proposal for indicative planning, including a project of that sort and made its intentions known to the provincial governments there would have been far less scurrying about in the backrooms of this house in the past few weeks as the administration sought to avoid a showdown with recalcitrant provinces. The governments of the provinces would realize they were expected to become part of a national plan and their justifiable demands for an increased share of investment capital would be met.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this organization entitled the economic council of Canada -I do not know what else you could call it- is merely going to be another of those farcical organizations we have had so often in the past. At best it will be a fact-finding statistic-collecting organization with no authority to present, institute or formulate any real economic plans. Anyway, there is no intention of having it do anything of that sort. As the foundation stone for economic planning in Canada it is as ludicrous and as inadequate

Economic Council of Canada as the proposal which was made by the previous government and which was so strenuously derided by the gentlemen now occupying the treasury benches.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with regard to the economic council, we may wonder, on the local, provincial or federal level whether we need such an instrument to help promote our economy.
To illustrate my views on our development and on regional issues, I should like to quote the following:
In such areas which, to a large extent, have been kept out of the economic advance, there is a recession not only in comparison to the remainder of the country, but sometimes even in the absolute sense. From year to year, life becomes more difficult there: The competition of powerful industries and prosperous farming in other areas gradually ruins the remaining industrial establishments, as well as farming and business. A spirit of revolt, the very opposite of the spirit of enterprise which alone could improve conditions, takes shape and develops. Slowly, and mostly unwillingly, the people leave those areas without a future to seek better opportunities in more dynamic parts where they sometimes create serious problems with regard to accommodation and employment.
It was on purpose, Mr. Speaker, that I did not indicate the source of that quotation at the start. Some people might think that it describes some of our underdeveloped areas. Well, it is an excerpt from the International Review of Social Sciences, UNESCO, No. 3, 1959, dealing with certain French areas which are faced with the problem of industrial centralization, and where the necessary steps were to be taken to give them a new start.
Now, that is about the same problem which is found in the lower St. Lawrence and many other of our districts. Such a situation may well cause some anxiety.
On the one hand, we see an increasingly larger part of our people getting used to put their trust in a welfare state, and, on the other hand, we have a group of citizens who are alarmed by the situation and try, generously, to give a new buoyancy to our economy and to fight that centralizing trend.
We are greatly concerned, because if we come to rely solely on the welfare state, stifling any initiative, growing accustomed to sponge on the state, since there is no other solution and that on the other hand, those who are struggling to give new impetus to the economy feel that they are ill-supported and ignored, it may happen that they will grow weary and that they will also follow the trend.
[Mr. Cameron (Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands) .1
In our area, we did not merely bemoan our lot nor blame our neighbours for our troubles. We deemed it necessary to form a group and to set up a district council of economic planning. It is the municipalities and the county councils which took the initiative, since industry lacked the required vitality to fill in the gaps. It was therefore necessary to rely on those whose duty it is to promote the public weal and to see to it that, instead of being constantly at strife, because everyone wants to have a finger in the pie, we should work together in good understanding in order to achieve our common aims in our given community. In this manner, a normal and constant development of our areas would be possible, so that instead of relying entirely on state assistance, we could proudly enable our people to earn a living.
This is an example of a community which may not be as privileged as others, but which accepted its responsibilities and preferred to unite rather than remain divided, and hired experts to conduct studies. We started by making a demographic survey, because it is the best way to know exactly what is our human potential, a most important point. We had a survey made on transportation by Mr. Pierre Camu, vice president of the St. Lawrence seaway authority, and also an investigation in the field of agriculture and of forestry, in order to know what our resources are and to be in a position afterwards to plan properly the development of our areas.
You have, on a higher level, the example of the province of Quebec which also felt the need to put its affairs in order. Our province provided for the establishment of a council of economic planning which could operate in a truly democratic fashion, without undue state control, but thanks to an indicative direction and planning. This was achieved through regular legislation providing financial incentives to those who wished to take part in the plan, thus permitting a more orderly development of Quebec's resources.
We feel that if that is a must on the local and provincial scenes, it is just as necessary at the federal level.
Who would build a house with foundations, walls and partitions without adding a roof?
We are a nation and as such we have obligations to fulfil and a part to play. Some will say, like the hon. member who spoke before me, that we will get nowhere unless

we resort to imperative planning. Others will claim that it would be better to leave things as they are, that everything will come out all right in the end. Others yet will raise various federal-provincial problems.
In my opinion, everyone must do his share in his own field. The fact remains however that the federal government has a great part to play in the field of transport, communications, public works, etc. Our efforts should be co-ordinated to give a boost to our economy.
Every one will agree also that we must try to co-ordinate the efforts of the regional and provincial economic boards so that there is no conflict between their different activities, which is the only way our country can grow in a normal and orderly fashion.
Of course, we must not exaggerate the importance of the economic council, since that is not the only solution. Several other measures dealing with the serious problem of unemployment and underdeveloped areas are now on the order paper. This piece of legislation is just one aspect of the over-all plan to facilitate the normal economic growth of our country.
I think the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) spoke for all our hon. friends opposite when he said one should take care not to rush into a marriage one might have cause to regret till the end of one's days. That, it seems to me, is typical of the attitude our hon. friends take when they are faced with the problems now before us, that is to say they have a way of flirting with problems without ever espousing them. I would even go as far as to say that is just like a young man who would be courting a girl and telling her in advance he has absolutely no intention of marrying her and who would still deny her the right to go out with another boy. Well, perhaps such a relationship can accidentally end up by creating something, but it is surely a sterile and irresponsible way of dealing with the problem at hand.
We on this side of the house want to espouse the cause of the unemployed, the cause of the depressed areas, and we know, because such is the law of nature, that childbirth cannot always be painless. Be that as it may, let us see to it that projects are carried out which will make the development of our country possible, even if, at first, that might hurt the feelings of some of our neighbours.
Everybody will agree that we must allow all people who are interested in the economic
Economic Council of Canada life of our country to group themselves, to unite, to make surveys and also to put forward programs which may help us to deal with the serious situation we are in.
To be constantly bringing up the problem of federal-provincial relations as an objection is to use a two-edged sword. Naturally, we can never care enough for the respect of provincial rights and especially those of the province of Quebec. Of course, we must allow that province to develop normally in the respect of all its rights.
On the one hand, feelings are aroused by the question of federal-provincial relations in the province of Quebec. On the other hand, the other provinces are led to believe that the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) is yielding to the pressure of the province of Quebec. But we must realize that we live in a pluralistic state, which means that there is a need for continuous negotiations. On that point, I should like to refer to the same book where we find, on pages 362 and 363, that in a pluralistic state:
-various other requirements must be fulfilled so that the necessary spirit of compromise and conciliation can be maintained. Population segments entirely deprived of power must not be numerous; the access to political life must be fairly easy; the various groups must be of a fairly equal strength, so that none of them can readily impose its will on others; finally, negotiations must be pursued unremittingly, with obstinacy and ability. We have seen that the maintenance of an order, whichever it is, always calls for a certain amount of energy; the maintenance of a pluralistic order entails enormous efforts in negotiations. Politicians being the true negotiators in pluralistic systems, every organization must have them at its disposal.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the man who succeeded at a critical and extremely difficult time, on the international level, in negotiating for the establishment of world peace, will succeed, on the national level, in negotiating the establishment of Canadian unity, with due respect for the individual rights and the interests of every Canadian.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND DEFINITION OF DUTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the minister is really anxious to see this economic council give good results, I am sure he will admit that it is imperative that this council, and consequently the federal government, secure full co-operation on the part of the provinces.
For example, paragraph (j) on page 4 of the bill states the following:
to seek full and regular consultation with appropriate agencies of the governments of the several provinces.

Economic Council of Canada
And, on page 4, paragraph (iv) of section 11 states:
the use of training programs at all levels of industry, and the use of retraining programs to meet changing manpower requirements.
I would ask the minister the following question: if he really wishes this legislation to work efficiently and to help promote the economic development of this country, why does the government obstinately refuse to submit it to the provinces at the federal-provincial conference which is to be held in a few days? I am asking this question with the utmost sincerity, since the federal government needs the provinces' and the municipalities' full co-operation if it wants this legislation to be fruitful. I should be very grateful if he would take a minute or two to give us a direct answer, and thus give assurance to the house that he will make all the necessary efforts so that the Canadian economy will derive all that it possibly can from this bill. I would be very happy if the minister could take a minute or two to give me an immediate answer to that question. What are the actual objections?
Mr. Speaker, since the beginning of this session, we have witnessed a complete invasion of the provincial field. Besides, some economists remind me of certain psychiatrists: the patient's mental and physical health often gets worse after the latter has been committed to their care. We do not wish to see that happen with the healthy autonomy of our provinces. We want the provinces to have complete jurisdiction in the labour-management field, and in all matters which come under provincial authority, such as natural resources, hydroelectric power, as well as numerous other fields, including agriculture.
Mr. Speaker, we are anxious to be told on what grounds the government obstinately refuses to consult the provinces.
Before promulgating ARDA, we consulted ail the provincial governments, and only with their full consent, did we enforce the act.
I feel that the bill providing for the establishment of an economic council of Canada should come under the Department of Trade and Commerce, or the Department of Industry. Whom does the government intend to appoint as chairman, directors and members of that council? Does it plan on selecting a fair percentage of representatives of our agricultural elite, of our labour force and of our managerial class?
Mr. Speaker, let us assume that one of our provinces, because it was not consulted, or

because it is jealous of its autonomy, chooses not to co-operate with the central government, or with the economic council. What then would be the latter's attitude? Would its action not be impaired, would our economy not be endangered?
I wonder also whether the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act-or ARDA-should not be under the jurisdiction of the projected economic council. ARDA has been operating in numerous countries, such as France for instance, and it has helped solve many problems, as it bears upon three technical fields: (a) the use and improvement of marginal lands; (b) rural development and industrial expansion; (c) land amelioration and soil conservation, water conservation and production.

Mr. Speaker, I think that ARDA can, from the economic point of view, assist greatly in relieving numerous problems which exist now in agriculture, more particularly in underdeveloped areas of this country. In my opinion, if this economic council of Canada really wishes to do efficient work, it must know the policy embodied in ARDA and work in close contact with it.
Mr. Speaker, I also believe that there is another serious problem, that is unemployment. Permit me to say incidentally that, according to the last statistics, unemployment is higher now than it was last year on this date. I am of the opinion that it is absolutely necessary to have the largest proportion of our raw materials processed in Canada.
As far as raw materials are concerned, grains as well as metals can be considered as raw materials.
It is a fine thing to sell our western grain abroad, but if that grain were processed in the east, the income of our farmers would be higher. In fact, this is why the Conservative government had prepared during the last session a piece of legislation providing for payment by the federal government for the transportation of grain from Fort William to eastern Canada. The same legislation provided for payment by the federal government

of the building cost of warehouses built along the waterways of eastern Canada in addition to the warehousing costs of cereals.
Mr. Speaker, the minister's speech was most interesting. I readily recognize it, as I often do not share his opinions, but I must admit that this speech was substantial.
He did a good job and I believe he is probably sincere when he advocates certain measures, regardless of the provinces' interest.
It is easier to work out a policy in some countries as, for example, in France, where you have a unified government, than in a country like ours, with a federal government and ten provincial governments. I admit that it is often difficult in our country to carry out an economic program. However, as long as the constitution has not been revised and amendments have not been brought to bear with the consent of all parties, in my opinion the minister must submit such a program to the provincial authorities to get efficient cooperation and work towards the national interest.
Those are, Mr. Speaker, the few remarks I wanted to make and I would be pleased if the minister could give us the reasons why he does not want to submit this bill to the provinces with a view to securing their full co-operation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill is part of a much advertised Liberal program of legislation, but in form it is merely a rewrite, with one addition, of two bills which were brought in by the former government. I refer particularly to Bill C-87, which was introduced on November 28, 1962, to establish a national economic development board, and to an act of parliament, the National Productivity Council Act, chapter 4 of the 1960-61 statutes. In addition to the combination of these bills there is a very greatly enlarged objective clause, which I believe makes the whole intent of this bill much different.
At this stage of our proceedings we cannot study the bill clause by clause. I do not wish to do so, but there are three particular parts of the bill that ought to be discussed, as each derives from a source which ought to be mentioned. There is first Bill C-87, and if we look at the bill before us we find that clauses 1 to 8 are identical with the clauses in Bill C-87, with the exception that the name has been changed from the national economic development board to the economic council of Canada, and the word "board" where it appears has been changed to "council". The
Economic Council of Canada only difference I can find is that the term of office of the chairman is to be seven years instead of ten years. Therefore we have no objection to this part of the bill and we think these clauses are worthy of support.
Clause 11 of the bill is lifted right out of the National Productivity Council Act. The words are identical and this portion of the bill is merely a reprint of the main and essential part of that act.
Clauses 12 to 20 are substantially the same as clauses 13 to 21 in the old bill, No. C-87. This leaves only clauses 9 and 10, which stipulate the duties of the council, where the difference in direction appears. The present bill looks something like the old bill, but its implications are much broader, and it is our view that it gives the council a stronger hold, almost an octopus hold, on the business and economic sectors of Canadian life.
When we come to these clauses on committee stage we will want to have some assurance from the minister as to the extent to which he intends to use these very broad powers that are given to the council. We will also want to make sure that the centralization of powers in Canada is not extended unduly, and in fact is not extended any more than is necessary for an over-all look at the Canadian economy.
What we fear most is not the actual wording of the bill but the theories behind it, which were expressed by the President of the Privy Council when he introduced it. We feel that they tend to show us that his intentions are to make this council one which will have a very strong bearing on business in Canada. We believe that business in Canada today appreciates assistance; they appreciate assistance in changing from one product to another; they appreciate assistance in improving their product and in marketing it. For these things they do look to government, and they were encouraged to look to government by the progressive legislation that our party brought before parliament. To this extent we are in sympathy with the purposes of the bill.
We think that any assistance whatever that can be given to Canadian businessmen, particularly in the export field, is well given. It is not within the competence of many Candian businesses, particularly the smaller ones, to go out into foreign fields and look for markets; they have to rely upon the services of such bodies as the Department of Trade and Commerce and the new council which will be established. To that extent we are not objecting to, and in fact we approve of the principle of this bill.
I think we should examine the theory and philosophy behind the changes that were

Economic Council of Canada put into this bill which amends the bill concerning the national economic development board. This bill, along with other government legislation, has been put forward as part of a program. We are told that this bill goes hand in hand with the department of industry bill, the capital development corporation bill, the Atlantic provinces development board bill and the municipal loans bill, to indicate a program of economic development to assist in relieving unemployment, and so forth. Mr. Speaker, we do not think this objective has been accomplished. We think that the program as a program was hastily thrown together; that it is composed of bits and pieces picked up here and there in order to present to the country quickly something that looks like a program. We think this bill particularly was merely derived from two or three sources, put together and announced as one of the great, new items of legislation of this government. We do not think this has in fact been accomplished.
We recall that when the department of industry bill was before the house the minister could not say, for example, how many people would be employed in the department or how much it would cost. He said this would depend pretty much upon the circumstances at the time. It was an indication of an intention to do something, without any well laid plans. I am not going to dwell on that matter now, Mr. Speaker. Hon. members opposite will say I am rehashing the old bill, and I do not wish to do that; I merely wish to deal with this particular bill. This was one aspect that bothered opposition members and on which a number of questions were asked; that is, what is this department doing; how many people are going to be employed, and how much is it going to cost? These questions could not be answered by the minister and therefore the house was left pretty much in the dark as to the intention of this bill.
We believe the same thing applies to the municipal loans legislation. I do not want to beat anybody over the head with the problem with which the government is faced in this regard, except to say that here again we think it is not part of a well planned and well laid out program. We think it was done hastily as part of a program to be laid before this parliament within 60 days in order that the government could fulfil their election promise. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we think the municipal loans bill, as part of this program, while it was well intentioned and may in the end work out properly, was not planned and put forward in the way it should have been.

The capital development corporation bill is not before us; it has not yet been discussed. However, I think it is perhaps in the same category. After reading the resolution we think this measure has not been planned and there is no over-all plan which will give assistance to the new economic council for Canada. The same remarks apply to the Atlantic provinces development board bill. There again it merely contains slight changes. A maximum amount of money was included as a provision of the bill, but we did not get any clear picture about who was going to be on this board or how it could be improved under the new legislation as compared with the old. We recall that the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Maclnnis) particularly asked the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) what plans he might have to assist in the development of the Atlantic area. The minister was unable at that time to say there was any plan, that he had anything to put forward. He just said, "We will wait and see what the board produces".
These are all rough sketches of the legislation we had before, Mr. Speaker. I am merely trying to prove the point that this economic council is not a great, new piece of Liberal legislation; it is merely a throwing together of two Conservative bills, one of which was passed and one of which was never passed, with expanded objects to which I shall refer in a few minutes. I mentioned that this bill eliminates the national productivity council and takes the heart, the main sections, out of the previous bill, puts them into this bill and sets up one council. There is only one thing in commendation that I wish to say to the government. I am glad they did not create two new councils. It is quite obvious that they intend to change the personnel of the productivity council, because when the bill before us is passed, the productivity council will come to an end; therefore the appointments which have been made will also come to an end and the government will be able to go ahead and make new appointments. I think possibly this is one of the main features of this new bill, as it was with the Atlantic provinces development board bill; that is, it is not in order to make any progress or because there is anything in either of these bills which could not have been done under the old bills; it is merely a case of passing a bill in order that the personnel may be changed and the government may put its own nominees on these boards. I think that is not sufficient reason for the government making a great fuss about the program they are putting forward. This bill will eliminate the productivity council and its members, as I have said. It is also an enlargement of the progressive

legislation already brought in. I believe the worst feature of the bill is that the central organization, the council, has been given such broad powers under this new bill that it can more than assist and advise, which the old bill only sought to do; it can now give some direction. This is the thin edge of the wedge to which we take objection. When we come to the clauses I intend to ask the minister if he will indicate clearly to the house how far he proposes to make use of clauses 9 and 10 and how far he expects that the council will be provided with funds and direction along these lines.
I hope it will not be said of me that I am afraid of progressive ideas. I am sure that one matter that is thrown back and forth from one corner of the house to another is that certain parties are afraid of progressive ideas and will vote against them. We are not afraid of progressive ideas; but if progressive legislation means more direction in Canada's economy, if progressive legislation means more centralizing of Canada's economy in one body in the federal field, then I do not believe this is progressive. I believe it is rather the opposite, that it is regressive; because in our British North America Act and most of our legislation we keep fighting against this tendency to have everything in this great country run from a central point. I hope that that is not the intention behind this bill.
I believe that at the moment what Canadian business wants most is to be left alone. I think that if it can be given some help to secure better products and better markets it will be pleased. But I do not think that it will welcome interference or direction. In the explanation of the bill which the minister gave us when introducing it, my definite impression is that he intended to make use of the bill to give direction. Certain statements and writings of his were read into the record to indicate his feeling that Canadian business could not look after itself, and that Canadian business had to be directed in some fashion in order to get the economy rolling. I say, Mr. Speaker, that if this is in fact what is intended it will not have that effect. Business is interfered with constantly, it seems, by every piece of legislation which is introduced. We all know that a good deal of the business personnel now engaged in each section of the Canadian economy spend a lot of their time answering government questionnaires and requests, complying with regulations, paying taxes and filing returns. This is so particularly with small businesses. I have received all sorts of complaints about organizations such as the dominion bureau of statistics, which is authorized to send out questionnaires to small businesses, and which can force the small businesses to answer these questionnaires. In the 28902-5-148
Economic Council of Canada case of a one-man business where the wife probably does the books, there just is not time to complete this sort of questionnaire. In the case of corporations, they must file tax returns and so forth, and fill in forms which emanate not only from the central government but also from the provincial and municipal governments. I think it is a common complaint among businesses large and small that government interference, government returns of one kind or another and government supervision is stifling the actual objective of these companies, which is to produce some product and put it on the market to sell. I saw a newspaper article recently which indicated that the percentage of people employed in office work is now increasing and the percentage of those employed in production decreasing. This is brought about to a large extent by the factors I have just mentioned, and government intervention in all these matters has caused a great deal of difficulty to small businesses.
I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that these theories of social and economic advances must be approached with caution. Last year I felt that the bill to establish the national economic development board went as far as it should have gone in the direction indicated by this new bill. Perhaps this new bill has gone too far, in that its direction is more intensified toward control of private business. We have to approach the matter with caution. We must not bring new ideas and specialized personnel to the point where they are devoting their efforts to non-productive objectives. I hope that the minister when he replies on second reading, or when we get to the committee stage, which we hope to do this afternoon, can assure us that this type of legislation and the work of this council will be approached in a cautious manner and that there will not be forced upon Canadian business another series of interferences by way of government forms and returns, and so forth, without an effective result being produced as far as business is concerned. If that assurance is given I see no reason why we should not support the bill.
Progressive legislation can be effective and useful if it is taken with caution. I do not want to mention any other matters, but matters have come before this house in recent weeks which a lot of us feel were brought about hastily and without proper thought. What we fear with regard to this bill is that in order to make a great impression on business and on the people the government will rush into interference with business in Canada in order to improve the employment situation and increase production and exports. Often if you rush into these things without proper groundwork being laid the effect is the absolute opposite of what was intended.

Economic Council of Canada We do not get the results intended by legislation already on our statute books, nor do we get the result intended by new legislation.
May I say in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that the former bill on the economic development board was a satisfactory step. As I have stated, there is only one objectionable feature in the new bill, and that is in clauses 9 and 10. In the old bill the clauses were very limited and were prescribed with caution. The wording was carefully considered to the point where the council could not misuse its powers of direction. I am afraid that the same caution has not been used in the drafting of this present bill, but if we have the necessary assurances from the minister we will be satisfied to support the principle of the bill, with some hesitation as to the government's intention.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great interest to the statement made by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Lamontagne) according to which the purpose of the economic council of Canada is to establish planning in our country. He also made a point of being explicit about the sort of planning he had in mind. In fact, the President of the Privy Council is an expert on planning fundamentals. When I see him, I am reminded of our great Quebec socialists. That is why we are always somewhat leery. Quebec is against all forms of socialism and the President of the Privy Council should know it since he has suffered two bitter defeats in his own city because of his ideas on centralization; he even had to go into exile in an English speaking riding.
When the President of the Privy Council uses the expression "indicative planning", I am yet confident. It even seems that he is trying to convince himself by repeating in his bill the words "assess, recommend, study, reexamine, analyse, encourage, initiate research," etc.
But I would advise him to be careful at all times on the brink of dangers he seems anxious not to reveal to the people. In fact, the government would have shown more respect for democracy if they had had two members appointed by each province and three by the federal government. Such a membership would be acceptable to all provinces and to all parties in the house. Thus they would have set up a national council representing all ten provinces.
So the objective of the economic council will be to study that grand system of supply and demand, resulting in all the various unpredictable up and down cycles, but


having a real cause nevertheless. It is that cause I want to discuss before the house.
When I see the President of the Privy Council consider only two parts of our economic system, I am always surprised to find that he does not go farther along those lines and does not use the third part of our present economic system. Is it a lack of agility? Perhaps he keeps that last ball up his sleeve, to keep us guessing. That is his secret. Nevertheless, that omission should not be made on purpose, let alone, rewarded.
Mr. Speaker, the possibilities of adaptation of our industries will be considered, and even the creation of new industries if possible. Very well.
When we deal with markets, I feel that we give too much importance to export industries and not enough to manufacturing industries capable of reaching the private market. Certainly we should think about exports, and we can even boast of being one of the largest exporting countries.
And despite the fact that Canada ranks fourth among exporting countries, our trade balance is becoming more and more unfavourable. Is that not food for thought for our economists? I am not an economist but I have enough common sense as far as administration is concerned to realize that, if I sell 50 per cent of the lumber on my woodlot to pay my suppliers and still owe more, my lot is not producing as it should, or expenses have got out of hand.
While, with our exports in relation to our population, we should have enormous surpluses, we find in the end that we have increasing deficits. The defect certainly goes deeper than exports themselves. This deficiency in our economy is that we have completely ignored the local market. Consequently, we have taken great care not to help, encourage, back, not to mention all the other words used by the minister, the market we have here, within our reach, the domestic market.
I want to point out that these last years, the federal government gave all the assistance that was needed to certain industries, mainly to those with foreign capital, based on our natural resources, and completely forgot the smaller industries which could do nothing else but barely carry on in this one-way economy.
I could not say what the minister thinks about this but I am sure he could not help seeing that deficiency.

However, I fear his cure. In any case, if a better physician cannot be found, I hope with all my heart that he will rectify a mistake by helping the industries which should have been the first concern of the past governments, private industries, family industries. Thus, he would, I think, apply the effective cure to our deficit of payments by renewing, modernizing, multiplying and creating, in some cases, numerous private industries which have been needed for over 20 years in order to meet consumer demand and supply the domestic market which is today out of our control in a proportion of 60 per cent.
In brief, Mr. Speaker, I feel it is urgent- and Social Crediters have been saying this over and over again for 25 years-to deal with the crucial problem of the processing industry in our country, without slowing down the growth of our big industry.
How many consumer goods are we obliged to import when it would be so easy to produce, manufacture and process them here?
I cannot go into details because I will do so when the bill is studied in committee, but you can see all the sectors that the processing industry could cover all over the country, thus giving work to thousands of workers who could more easily consume all the goods manufactured in our country.
In spite of what our good economists say, we Social Crediters remain convinced that the great ill of the day is the lack of purchasing power due to a faulty distribution of credit.
As long as our modern economy rests solely on supply and demand, without taking into account capital and distribution, we will go from recession to recession every three or four years at the whim of those who control the faucet of our credit and of our system of distribution.
Since it is mostly concerned with exports, our big industry will continue to have a surplus of production at certain intervals because there is not enough variety at the secondary level of industry and it will be our small industries which will suffer the most from that situation.
I wonder if the President of the Privy Council ever asked himself the following question. Would it not be those who control our monetary system who cause those ups and downs, those alternating periods of surplus and restriction?
28902-5-148J
Economic Council of Canada
When, for instance, your business has been going well for three or four years and everybody is working, the bank suddenly tells you that it must cut off your credit, and you wonder why, but the only answer you get is that banks have decided to do so all over the country.
Everybody must accept that decision, private individuals, provincial governments and even the federal government.
That is why encyclicals state that those who control credit and money also control the lives of people.
Yet, we look for an answer, we examine the situation and we nationalize everything that comes under provincial jurisdiction. We are so anxious to solve the problem that we no longer even hear the protests of the provinces. Are we not doing the same thing as the foolish virgins of the gospel?
Let us put our house in order before we start telling the provinces that they are unable to solve the problem of unemployment.
Actually, unemployment is not a problem at all; it is just the normal consequence of undue interference on the part of the central government.
What our major concern should be under the present circumstances is to nationalize bank credit.
That would keep the great centralizers busy for a while. Let them start by centralizing credit. Let them give back to the Bank of Canada the exclusive powers of making and issuing all credit across Canada.
In the industrial field you will admit that some industries in the present situation must be guided by the state and even state controlled.
In the monetary field, you will admit also that eight private companies are able to issue, on behalf of the state, the credit which represents its face value, its actual wealth.
I do not understand you or I understand you too well. Spelling out the facts might be the greatest scandal against the state and the people.
You remind me of a milk producer who wonders what to do with its product while consumers are waiting for it to survive. Everybody starves because our producer decided against the use of a delivery man to take it to the consumers.
Is it because they do not understand or is it because they are paid not to understand?

Economic Council of Canada That is the question we have the right to ask ourselves with respect to this government.
You persist in saying that the logical system of Social Credit is not feasible- because it does not suit the modern financiers and our would-be millionaires. But, at least, find a better one. And stop clowning in front of the people in order to distract their attention from the truth.
Those really responsible for our unappealing economy are not up on the moon. They are right here. They are the government and all the successive governments which sold out to big finance, and which are still living off the traitor's pay-off, surrendering their country to some financiers from whom they have accepted blood money.
The great remedy would be a nationalist government which would operate, at last, in the interest of the people who elect them and not of American finance.
Mr. Speaker, we are first of all for private enterprise, and we consider every act of the government as bringing assistance to that private enterprise.
Today, times have changed, and production must adapt to our atomic era and for that purpose, governments must support the almost superhuman efforts of private enterprise.
As for this bill, the federal government must give assistance, provided that doing so it does not violate any statute.
Under the pretense of playing the good Samaritan the federal government should not infringe upon the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces.
If the chairman of the future economic council abides by the standards stipulated in the bill, then we will be confident that this organization will be of valuable assistance in the improvement of our Canadian economy.
I would even dare ask something of the president. I acknowledge his high qualifications as a rational and enlightened economist, but I should like him to be a little more daring and I want to repeat this, I should like him to be a little more daring in his future research. In a word, would he stop just looking at facts? I have already seen many other economists doing just that.
I believe, sir, that your years of being factual are behind you and that your new duties require broader views. Stop being contemplative and initiate the new economic discoveries our country needs so urgently. Break away from the narrow framework of partisan philosophy and think of the greatness of our country.


I am not prone to condemn at first sight. That is why I will have faith in the new council.
I am sure that the government will be able to take advantage of all the suggestions put forward in this debate.
Let us not forget that the federal government has been created by the provinces and that it will not be able to work seriously and efficiently unless it obtains full co-operation from the ten provinces.
The objective of the government, namely to create a system of economic planning in Canada, with close consultation with the provinces and the private sector of our economy, is most commendable.
We hope, for the minister's sake, that we will not have to wait too long for the desired results in the best interests of the labour force of this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take up a great deal of the time of the house today speaking on this bill. The subject, however, is a very important one. The scope for debate is very broad. This subject has recently occupied a great deal of our attention during the last two election campaigns, when it was mentioned from almost every platform in the country. I am sure it is a subject that is dear to the hearts of all Canadians, particularly since they have been somewhat frightened, bewildered and misled by the barrage of propaganda directed at them from the Liberals during the last two campaigns. The Liberals have been telling the people what a terrible state the country is in because of the Conservative government we have had for the last few years.
The purpose of this bill is to establish a council which will take a good look at the economy and report on the state of the economy. The Liberals would much prefer that any such report were given to them in private rather than to the public because they would much prefer to dispense their own kind of misinformation to the Canadian people. They have found it pays; they would not be in office if they were not so successful in selling this misinformation. However, I do not want to rehash the last two election campaigns. I do believe that we have had perhaps too much propaganda and not enough analysis of the factors in those parts of Canada's economy where the government can be useful.
A casual look at the subject will indicate the many roles a government can play. I am

sure that those of us who believe in private enterprise are not at all interested in trying to get the government into business any more than is absolutely necessary. We believe in the maxim that the best government is the one which interferes the least. However, the modern world in which we live and the competition from other nations, makes it almost impossible for an industry in Canada today to survive and expand as it must without some help from the government. Other nations have their industries regimented, assisted or controlled by the government. They are financed by the government. The laws of the country are made to assist these industries to export their goods. Whether we like it or not, therefore, in order for Canadian business to have a chance to compete the government must assist in some ways.
Some of this assistance, of course, has to be in the form of a guard against the harmful effects of governmental action by other countries, and the influence they have on their own industries and their own exports to this country. Some of the effects we must have would take the form of financial assistance to our own exporters who want to enter markets where the purchaser might not be financially sound or where the cash to purchase the goods is not readily available.
I am sure that we should have spent much more time in considering the fact that Canada is just a new manufacturing nation. We should have considered the fact that, while we are very proud of what we have in this country, generally as a nation we had had much less need for education in order to get along. The educational standards of Canadians, therefore, have been very low. If we had considered all these facts, we would have realized some of these fundamental difficulties a little quicker than we did. I am just citing this as one example of the way in which the government could have used a little more foresight, and I am wondering if there are similar areas in which foresight could have been used. We discovered, almost belatedly, that we did not have a pool of skilled workers. We started to try to change this country from a producer of raw materials to a manufacturing economy. We started to build new plants and found we did not have the skilled tradesmen necessary to man those plants. We started a crash program to train them. Now I suggest that if there had been more imagination, more consideration of what I call the fundamentals of Canada's economy, whether it be by a skilled advisory group or by a government, we would not have been so late in recognizing the need for these skilled tradesmen.
I am happy to think that the problem of Canadian ownership of industry is receiving
Economic Council of Canada attention. I was glad to see that the government was quick to withdraw the method by which it was suggested they would do something about it. Certainly, the fundamental point here is that you do not get people to do things by punishing them if they do not. You encourage them to do what you think is best for the country. If there is one thought I may give the house today in this respect, it is this point of the encouragement of Canadian ownership. Obviously if the country is going to change from a producer of raw materials to a manufacturing economy, large amounts of capital have to be found. If these large amounts of capital are to be imported, then we are going to have a good percentage of our means of production owned outside the country.
The alternative is to turn the Canadian from being a saver into being an investor. Canadians are too cautious, too slow to invest, too careful of their dollar. We must show a little more daring. The only way you can encourage this is by giving rewards for investment. I would suggest the only way this can be done is to put in a new incentive for the wage earner, put him in a new tax bracket if he invests a certain percentage of his earnings per year. This might be done through a payroll deduction plan. Let us offer companies these same tax concessions to spread out their shareholdings amongst many more Canadians. Every time they sell more stock in a company give them a special tax concession. Let us tie it all together with a buy-Canadian program. By laying stress on these things, we will give encouragement rather than discouragement. Perhaps we will start tackling these fundamental problems in the right way. I hope that those on the treasury benches, and this council when it comes into being, will at least consider this method I have suggested.
