speechtext:
I just wish to say, Mr. Chairman, that there has been a great deal said about economic planning and about the future of Canada during the course of this debate. The debate has ranged, on the one hand, from calling this legislation utterly useless and insipid, to calling it dangerous
[Mr. Gregoire.l

and dictatorial on the other. Taking a strictly objective and constructive view so far as the setting up of this economic council is concerned, I say it can render a great deal of good and a genuine service to Canada if certain precautions are heeded and a few fundamental changes are made to several of the sections.
There can arise real areas of conflict between the economic council of Canada and other regional and provincial economic councils, such as the Atlantic development board. In my opinion there is a real and pressing need in two areas so far as the function of the council is concerned. First it involves overall co-ordination and interlocking with provincial and regional economic boards and councils, and second there is a need to bring about a greater degree of co-operation and understanding between management, labour and government.
The greatest danger we see at the senior level of government is that it will appropriate to itself the sole responsibility for the creation and execution of all plans. In this respect I would like to read a portion of an editorial which appears on page 32 of the July issue of Canadian Business. This article is very timely, and it says under the heading "Too Much Government Elbowing":
The greatest danger we face is that our senior levels of government will appropriate to themselves sole responsibility for the creation and execution of all plans. It is still timely to remind ourselves that the prime responsibility of government should remain the clear delineation of long range objectives and the revamping of the financial and commercial structure through appropriate changes in taxes, tariffs, combines legislation and the like, to create an economic climate that encourages and prods private industry into constructive expansionary programs. If it is true, as indicated in the speech from the throne, that these are "times of great change throughout the world" when "the task before us is to seek out with wisdom and imagination, those new paths that will surely lead us forward," it is also true that the need for business to maintain maximum flexibility and freedom of choice is equally imperative. This requirement is not fulfilled by governments vying with each other to erect a multiplicity of new administrative bodies and to assume financial responsibility for activities now largely and more properly the responsibility of the private sectors of the economy . . . National and provincial attitudes with respect to taxation, industry rationalization, welfare, financial and fiscal policies all need to be formulated and pursued in a manner that aids and not hinders Canada's drive toward our minimum growth objective.
In this legislation we must have a guarantee that there will be full consultation with proper representatives of labour and management before instituting production expansion and research programs. What incentives for co-operation are there if the reports are to be withheld and if the findings of the council are not to be published? The question is simply, how do labour and management have

a hand in planning productivity and assistance programs if they are to be removed or elbowed out from the carrying out of programs introduced by the council, and which are taken over by the government? I think we should bear this in mind as we go through the clauses of the bill.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND DEFINITION OF DUTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, planning has become fashionable but even though it is fashionable there is no reason it should not be examined. It seems to me there was much lacking in this debate, but the problem we are facing is a serious one for the country. This country must grow economically at a faster rate than it has been growing.
In certain parts of the house there is a feeling that we should go back to the free, automatic, self-correcting market, but this market does not exist any more. Since the days of Sir John A. Macdonald we have always interfered with the development of business in our national policy. We have directed business in certain channels, we have provided avenues for business to develop in, and have provided a climate in which investment can come to Canada.
Mr. Chairman, as our country has developed in two world wars we have come to a stage of industrial maturity more akin to that of the United States. At the present time our economy and state of industrial maturity are more similar than ever before in our history. One further illusion has been destroyed; that is, that the more dissimilar are our economies, the more our trade is increased. We have to create in Canada a proper framework in which business can develop and prosper.
There is a view that our future can be both bright and haphazard. This is a mischievous idea. We certainly knew in the depression of 30 years ago that the so-called free market could exact too great a price. The unregulated market can be unstable, it can be capricious, it can be irrational. This is not good enough. We now have economic tools which we and others have developed, that can be used to guide the development of our economy, to lead us to higher economic plateaus and, to provide a greater abundance for the people of Canada. In providing this economic context one of the things we have done is provide welfare payments, social insurance benefits, social assistance, health and welfare services, from all levels of government amounting to $3,300 million a year. This was the figure in 1961, which was 11 times what we had paid in the immediate post-war years. This is not only a great social advance but it helps provide a market; it helps provide an
Economic Council of Canada economic context in which business can develop. This represents an important social revolution and is a compelling economic fact. The key to economic growth is profitable investment.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to quote from a study made by the international labour organization, published in 1961, by a group of experts one of whom was Professor Benjamin Higgins of McGill University. It says this:
The experts' analysis of the nature of the problem confirms the belief that lack of employment opportunities is due largely to capital shortage. In their view policies for proper utilization of labour must therefore centre mainly on ways of increasing investment and of making the best use of such capital as countries have or can obtain.
The first requirement is to raise the level of investment. As employment opportunities increase, the living standards of those who would otherwise have remained unemployed or underemployed will rise and there will be an urgent need for larger supplies of food and other necessities.
The key to economic growth is investment. We must provide more job opportunities; we must provide 250,000 additional jobs each year in this country. We have the resources, we have the manpower and the plant. We must now direct our economic activities into channels which will provide a greater rate of economic growth. Total new capital outlays reached a peak in 1957, declined in subsequent years through 1961, but rose again in 1962 and appear to be going upward again in 1963. These totals, however, are not sufficient to create a level of full employment in this country. We have in Canada half a million unemployed. If we are to create a higher level of employment we must encourage the mobilization of our economic forces and create a greater flow of investment capital in order to accelerate our rate of economic development.
This bill is to call together, to negotiate, to talk to people who are concerned with planning. We are planning at all levels of government; we are planning in business. It is a matter of getting an over-all umbrella for the co-ordinating of a plan of economic development. This matter has urgency; this matter has importance; this matter is a challenge to Canada and is a step along the road to an over-all plan for the economic well-being of Canada, in co-operation with the provinces, municipalities and business. It opens up new opportunities for the development of this country.

speechtext: Shall clause 1 carry?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND DEFINITION OF DUTIES
speechtext:
No, Mr. Chairman. There are a few general remarks I should like to make on the bill and which we would have made on second reading except that we thought it
2322	HOUSE OF
Economic Council of Canada preferable to have second reading and make these remarks at the committee stage.
As has already been pointed out, the bill is really almost identical to the one brought before us by the previous government, which bill at that time intended to set up the national economic development board. There are two major changes in it, the enlarging of the permanent staff of one to three, which is a distinct improvement, and the arrangement for a greater amount of publication of some of the studies which the board will carry out. This in itself is, again, an improvement and is welcomed. However, beyond that point there is really not a great deal of difference between the two bills, unless the minister can draw some matters to our attention which have escaped our notice to this point.
My chief reason for wishing to participate in this debate is to deal with some aspects of the minister's speech when introducing the measure on second reading. The speech itself was an interesting one. Knowing the calibre of the minister and his general economic reputation, we expected nothing less from him. It was interesting chiefly because it was one of the few occasions when anyone in the chamber has attempted to substantiate by some reasonable, economic arguments the planning attitudes of the government. We have had a great deal of discussion from the Conservative party about regimentation, interference with individual rights, and all that sort of nonsense. But the minister's speech was a rational attempt to economically explain their position on planning. As I say, Mr. Chairman, we expected nothing less from him, knowing his reputation.
I would like to deal with some of the points he raised because we in this party feel that the attitude he expressed is to some degree economically unrealistic and is a misrepresentation-not an intentional one-of the positions and policies we have advocated in this and other debates when similar economic measures have been under consideration.
In his speech the minister spoke of two types of planning. He first spoke of what he called indicative planning, and then of imperative planning. I think we should make it perfectly clear for the record that this bill does not provide either indicative planning or what the minister calls imperative planning. The minimum requirements of good, effective indicative planning is a planning board that will use all the advanced technological facilities at the disposal of the economists and that, after its studies are completed, will come up with a picture of the economy of the country as they would like it to be; a picture of the economy that will use the input and output table analysis, that will show


the desired levels of production and the breakdown of the desired levels by industrial sectors, that will trace back how these can be developed. These tables will affect the employment of manpower and the location and distribution of capital investment. This picture of the economy is then made available to the country and to industry generally, and it is hoped they will use this picture or plan of the economy to guide their investment policies and to regulate the scope of their own economy. In short, it is hoped that the economic sectors of the economy, industry and other people involved will co-operate with regard to the levels of employment and investment which are envisaged in the government's plan and go beyond the levels of economic growth.
An analysis of this bill makes it perfectly clear that it does not even go that far. I know that at the conclusion of his speech the minister spoke of the necessity for devising a plan of economic development. That is not in the bill. Its terms of reference are very vague. It seems to be largely a factfinding, information-gathering, information-co-ordinating agency. As the council develops under the guidance of the minister, perhaps he will be able to turn it into a proper agency of indicative planning. We very much hope that this will be the case, but as it stands at the present time the bill does not provide for indicative planning as understood by economists and as indicative planning takes place in other countries of the world.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands dealt this afternoon in some detail with some of the indicative planning which has been done in France and the amazing amount of success which has followed it. For the information of members of the Conservative party who were very worried about infringement on the rights of big business and private enterprise, it is interesting to note that in France when indicative planning was commenced the business community were opposed to it. But then as they appreciated its advantages and the way it could assist them, people in private enterprise are now its proponents and some of its major supporters. When you examine our proposals in comparison with proposals in other countries of the world, Mr. Chairman, you will realize how weak this council will be. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands pointed out that the section of the French plan which prepared indicative planning has a permanent staff of 50 with casual employees numbering in the hundreds in order to draw up the type of indicative plan which is needed. Under this bill we have three permanent people, some part time directors and presumably some staff; but our

suggestion is that this type of organization is totally incapable of doing even the indicative planning of which the minister spoke.
The real tragedy of this is that good indicative planning does work. If you prepare a plan of your economy as you want it to be, and if the industries of the country are convinced that the proper amount of research, accurate information and the proper amount of time has gone into drawing up such an economic plan, probably at least 50 per cent of it will be effective. Our main objection is that unless you are prepared to add on to your general plan some agency to ensure that it is carried out, then the general effectiveness of the plan itself is greatly diminished.
The other matter the minister spoke about was what he called imperative planning. This is nothing but a straw man set up by the minister, which he immediately proceeded to knock over. It is a caricature of our position to suggest that the detailed over-all planning that we advocate requires a daily, detailed intervention by government in each sphere of economic activity. To some extent, as I have said, well prepared indicative planning does work if it is a genuine plan. It works even better if the sectors of the economy which are involved know that behind the desire for co-operation lies a mechanism which, if necessary, can be used to see that the plan is carried out. If plans are to be effective governments must be prepared to intervene at critical points in the economy to ensure that the plans are carried into effect. If you are not prepared to do that, Mr. Chairman, then you are just playing around with the whole concept of planning. If your economic plan provides the mechanism to see that it is carried out, you will never need to use it in 90 per cent of the cases, because if it is an effective plan which can be consummated by the government, private industry will go along with it and you will not be required to interfere in those sections of the economy.
The minister said in his speech that one reason he is opposed to imperative planning is that he does not think that imperative planning could work in an industrial society. He stated that this was an acceptable form of planning for underdeveloped areas but that it would not work in an industrial society. All the minister is saying in that sentence really is that in our industrial society as we know it now the existing power groups are already so strong and so well-entrenched that it would be very hard to deal with them. But whether the government plans or not, whether it leaves it to the spheres of private enterprise, planning does take place. If it is
Economic Council of Canada not done by the government in the interests of all the people, then it is done by private enterprise in its own interests. That is the complaint that we make with the statement made by the minister in introducing this bill.
The private sections of our economy plan for their own welfare, and plan very inefficiently. As far as I am concerned, I cannot understand why governments are not prepared to step in and protect the interests of the community as a whole. When a government steps in to see that a plan for the general welfare of the whole community is carried into effect, you are not at that stage interfering with the rights of private corporations; you are affirmatively asserting the rights of individuals in the community in general rather than interfering with the private rights of corporations.
The minister further said that effective planning or imperative planning would involve wage and price controls. With all due respect, Mr. Chairman, that is nonsense. All you are doing with effective economic planning is controlling investment. Effective economic planning deals mainly and exclusively with the proper location of investment in the economic sphere of the country. For example, the minister said it would not work because we have a mixed economy in Canada. This again is not so. The mixed economies of Europe have had to use many of the planning techniques we in this party have advocated over the years, and they are working very well. So that a mixed economy can be adapted to the whole concept of proper and effective economic planning.
The minister also said that effective economic planning could not be used because we are living in a federal state, with the provinces having their own jurisdictions and their own areas of operation. This is a real problem. No economist could afford to ignore or overlook it. But surely the real problem is this, that our governments in the past have never really tried to solve the problems we face as far as the federal structure of Canada is concerned. We have always said that planning has to be federal, provincial, and much of it also municipal. The real difficulty is not hiding behind the problems which confederation creates but in trying to sit down, in co-operation with our provincial and municipal groups, and see that the present institutional and jurisdictional situations are developed in such a way that our planning can be effective.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands pointed out how the pensions scheme, if properly used, could provide a tremendous fund which could be allocated among our provinces. Once you begin federal planning you begin to draw in provincial

Economic Council of Canada bodies. They begin to co-operate in your schemes. You begin to draw in your municipal organizations. What we in Canada need is a permanent secretariat dealing with provincial and municipal matters. Perhaps we even need a minister of state for the provinces. Perhaps our provinces need departments of federal relations. But certainly the difficulty is not going to be solved merely by saying that our federal constitution makes effective and proper planning impossible. This is not so. What is required is to get into the whole field of economic planning, and then you will find that many of your constitutional difficulties will prove to be imaginative. The minister spoke of a plan. But that is not in the bill. Maybe he will tell us what authority is in the bill for drawing up such a plan. We should like to see it. He spoke about implementing a plan. We would like to know how. If the government is not prepared to intervene in the economy, how could it ever implement such a plan completely? Is it merely intending to rely on the co-operation of the people concerned?
In conclusion I should like to say a word in explanation of why we have been so insistent on discussing planning in this debate. When one examines the broad field of Canadian affairs he begins to realize how many matters await attention of governments both federal and provincial. There is, for example, chronic unemployment, the misallocation of investment, the lack of social capital to carry out important and necessary works, the slowness of regional development, the fluctuations in the business cycle of which the minister spoke and its reaction on our economy, the slow rate of growth and the fantastic changes which are taking place in the pattern of world trade. We believe that proper planning really can pursue the goal of full employment without endangering the balance of payments situation. We have been asking ever since this house assembled for some clear statement by the government on its trade policy. It is only by means of proper economic planning that we can really analyse our economy, find out what industries can compete in world markets and which are so inefficient that they cannot do so. It is only by means of proper economic planning that we can provide a scheme of adjustment assistance to industries which need such assistance during a period of transition. We are faced with all the difficulties posed by automation. We have to contend with a situation where so many of our assets are under foreign control. We must recognize that there is in Canada a lack of economic democracy- in practice the consumer has no rights, and no say about what is put on the market. His opinions are, in any case, created by the mass

media. There is still educational inequality. Does anyone in his right mind believe that all these things can be tackled and put to rights unless there is an over-all plan for Canadian development which would marshal all our resources, decide what we are capable of producing and determine how Canada can fit into the pattern of world trade?
I wish to emphasize once again that with the best intentions in the world this poor economic council will not be able to remedy this situation. It has neither the power nor the authority necessary to do even the elementary work of indicative planning, much less to see that the plans made are carried into effect.
Of course, the proposal represents a step forward and we intend to support it. We hope the chairman will take this council and make something of it. If this is done, perhaps in the years ahead Canada can move into the modern world of economic planning and take her place among some of the more progressive and forward looking nations of the world.

I was glad to see the words of commendation used by the Secretary of State last evening with reference to the co-operative attitude shown by the house, but I think this is one occasion when it is impossible to accede to the request which has just been made, much as I would like to do so. In any event, there will be a good deal of discussion on this subject. I am very anxious to hear the President of the Privy Council as he gives us, as I am sure he will, the philosophy which will animate the government in connection with the operation of this economic council. We are as desirous as can be of hearing the hon. gentleman translate the philosophy in the book which was mentioned-I gave only part of the name when I referred to it in the house; I gave the second part of the name and left out the major part. I noticed on examination of Hansard that the hon. gentleman asked me a question, a question I did not hear, as to whether or not I would give the full name of the book. Anyway, I am

sure the hon. gentleman will wish to elucidate .some of his philosophy. We have been anxious to hear him translate into concepts for parliament the general views expressed by him during the days when he represented the tribune of the Liberals.
